Richard I, widely known as Richard the Lionheart, was King of England from 1189 to 1199. Famed for his military prowess, he spent the vast majority of his reign abroad, principally leading the Third Crusade and defending his continental territories. Although a legendary figure of chivalry, his campaigns left England heavily taxed and financially drained, a burden that would fall on his successor.

Richard was a key commander of the Third Crusade, winning major victories at Acre and Arsuf against Muslim forces. Yet for all his military genius, he failed to recapture Jerusalem from Saladin, leaving the great objective of the crusade unrealized. On his return from the Crusade, his troubles multiplied. He was captured by Duke Leopold of Austria and held for ransom, a massive sum that nearly bankrupted the English treasury. During his decade-long reign, Richard famously spent less than a year in England itself, declaring at one point that he would sell London if he could find a buyer to fund his crusade.

His military career ended when he died from an infected crossbow wound received while besieging the minor castle of Chalus-Chabrol in France. He was succeeded by his younger brother John, who had tried to usurp the throne during Richard's captivity, taking advantage of his absence to consolidate power. His father had been Henry II, against whom Richard had repeatedly rebelled, allying with Philip II of France in dynastic struggles. His legacy remained that of a warrior king whose romantic appeal outlasted his actual achievements.
